t111_c3_illwill: In one of the Buddha’s own accounts of how he woke up, ill will shows up in his mind and he sees it’s hurting him. If he had to figure that out by watching, it’s not obvious. Ill will can make you feel powerful. Being on fire would too, and people would definitely get out of your way, but unless you’re the Human Torch from the Fantastic Four, you’d be the one burning. Has it ever left anybody at ease, with nothing to regret afterward?
t111_c4_borrowlove: Or put somebody you care about into your exact life, your family, your bank account and all, and then step outside it and ask what you’d tell them. It’s a cheap trick for becoming the outsider to your own mess. And the gap it gets around even has a name, Solomon’s paradox, after the king everybody brought their disputes to, who then wrecked his own life.
t111_c5_rogers: You can see the same move in a dramatized scene from the movie A Beautiful Day in the Neighborhood. Lloyd, a reporter, tells Mr. Rogers, “I can’t imagine it was easy… growing up with you as a father.” He doesn’t collapse under that or fight it, but he does answer what’s worth answering in it. He tells Lloyd that until recently his oldest son never told people about his dad, and his youngest “genuinely tested” him. Eventually he and his youngest found their way, and now he’s very proud of both his sons. Then he says, “But you are right, Lloyd. It couldn’t have been easy on them. Thank you. Thank you for that perspective.”
t111_c6_hook: When you catch it, look around and just take a moment to enjoy some free honesty: “Oh! I’m hooked again! That’s awesome I could notice it!” Take a breath or three before you finish whatever you were doing. Maybe then you’ll find there’s enough adult around to be nice to your little boo for a second. Or enough Protector to stop something you’d regret later.
t111_c8_belonging: Part of building who you are is untangling yourself from whatever pulls you away from your own knowing in return for belonging. A political tribe might expect consistent positions and predictable reactions, while a family or religion that’s kind to you might have expectations that just feel like being good. Most groups expect some conformity. Your family might want a particular kind of son or daughter, and your friends might have rules about what you can joke about or get upset about. But if going along means betraying yourself, that’s the bargain. It can help to write down the rules your family ran on, including unspoken ones like “Boys don’t cry.” Then write down the role you got handed, like the stand-in parent, or the one who got blamed for everything (ST-CA has lists of both, in sections 15.2.3 and 15.2.4).
t111_c9_beginner: Give a new interest enough tries to get past the humiliation of being a beginner, when you keep telling people, “Sorry, I’m new.” Maybe after that you still genuinely dislike it, and then you may quit. You may also discover a part of yourself that never had permission to exist.
t111_c10_people: Reparenting is usually talked about as something you do alone, or with a therapist. But your little one got hurt by people, so some of the healing has to happen with people too. Often it’s mostly one person carrying a lot of it, maybe the one who drives you to your appointments and says it’ll be okay. Maybe you’re picturing them right now. Having someone like that while you’re struggling can be an enormous blessing. If it’s more distributed, with various people you can count on for small parts, that can be more sustainable, even if it doesn’t feel as monumental.
t111_c10_calendar: Over time, reparenting can help you take in some of what they’ve been doing for you, and start doing it yourself, even that calendar bit. What you’re after is care your little one can count on from more than one place, while the inner relationship stays precious and important. Other jobs can go to friends or community, outsource to the tools or pros, whatever works. You’ll find the balance is dynamic between inner & outer reliance, and going too far in either extreme isn’t generally the healthiest.
t111_c11_forgive: For many people, healing does get around to some forgiveness eventually, or at least to not being run by the resentment anymore. It can’t be put on a schedule. And you don’t have to forgive first to get safe, set boundaries, hold someone accountable, get justice or get better. Then again, active resentment narrows what you see, and your little one stays organized around the injury. And if someone pressures you into forgiving early, what you get is an enlightened-looking act, with the wound gone underground.
t111_c12_missing: All of this happens in you, so it doesn’t matter whether they get any of it. And if it starts making you more compulsive, or a bit unreal, so you can’t get back to your life, make it simpler: “I miss you, and I care.” Some of that same care can go to the part of you that’s still here.
t111_p2_trackrecord: How do you check that? I’d keep what you feel around them in mind, and look at their track record too. Do they respect a no, or keep pushing on it, and what happens when you disagree? If something outside of them backs up what they’re telling you, and it all adds up, that’s a good sign.
t111_p5_son: A real-life child of yours, or a calm pet, can also act as a companion that brings out the relationship with your own inner child. My son did that for me, and I think that’s very common for parents. But those are also their own beings with their own needs as well. Let them come and go without making them responsible for the session.
t111_jl1_steadier: On a steadier day, when thinking about other people won’t pull you out of your own shoes, name the feeling plainly (lonely, say) and think of how many people are feeling that exact thing right now, and wanting it to stop, just like you. With that many people feeling the same thing, the theory that you’re the defective one gets kind of hard to keep up. Wish all of you, you first, enough support to stay with it, so the pain stops with you.
t111_q1_truce: Taking the hostility out makes room for warmth. Once a truce is made, we can begin to let down our defenses. I mean by choice, after the part guarding you has been heard. If you’ve never been safe being loved, your ego can act like a rigid security guard that won’t let the feeling in, and being vulnerable is the opening the feeling needs. (This guard is only about letting the feeling in. People still have to earn your trust.) Sometimes the warmth is there, with a cold part standing in front of it, guarding something. That part tends to step aside once it’s been heard (see the section Hear the Guard First).
